screens.title: Network Security in VPC
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll build a mental model for how AWS protects network traffic inside your VPC. You'll learn the two complementary layers of defense: Security Groups, which guard individual instances and are stateful, and Network Access Control Lists, which guard entire subnets and are stateless. We'll also cover how VPC Flow Logs let you monitor ACCEPT and REJECT events, which is essential for diagnosing blocked traffic. Throughout, I’ll use a building security analogy: Security Groups are the guards on each office door, and NACLs are the checkpoints at a floor entrance. That analogy helps explain why one is stateful and the other is stateless, why Security Groups only have allow rules, and why NACLs support explicit denies and rule ordering. By the end of the chapter you will be able to design a simple secure architecture for a public web tier and a private database tier, configure the Security Groups and NACLs to match that design, and use Flow Logs to verify whether traffic is being accepted or rejected. Consider how a single rejected flow can show you whether the subnet boundary or the instance firewall is responsible — that distinction is the core insight we’ll practice.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Network Security in VPC
Network Security in VPC
How Security Groups, Network ACLs, and VPC Flow Logs combine to protect instances and subnets, and how to design rules that avoid common connectivity failures.
In this lesson
Differentiate Security Groups vs NACLs; configure both; use Flow Logs.
Why it matters
Correct layering prevents easy exploits and avoids inadvertent outages from stateless rules.
Outcome
Design a public web + private DB setup with working SGs, NACLs, and Flow Logs for verification.
Concept map
Security Groups (stateful) → Instance guard. NACLs (stateless) → Subnet checkpoint. Flow Logs → audit trail.
Explore Key Topics
Security Groups — Instance-level, stateful, allow-only rules.
NACLs — Subnet-level, stateless, allow/deny, ordered.
VPC Flow Logs — Capture ACCEPT/REJECT metadata for analysis.

screens.title: Learning Objectives

You will configure Security Groups to control inbound and outbound traffic for EC2 instances and other resources, and you will implement NACLs at the subnet boundary to add an extra stateless layer of defense. You will learn best practices for using both together so they reinforce rather than conflict, and you will enable and interpret VPC Flow Logs to verify whether traffic was accepted or rejected. Each objective builds practical capability: recognizing when a connection failure is due to a NACL rather than a Security Group, writing least-privilege rules for SSH and service ports, and designing a public web plus private database pattern that follows AWS best practice. These are hands-on skills you will practice with specific rule examples and a troubleshooting scenario, so you can both design secure networks and diagnose real connectivity problems quickly.

screens.title: Security Groups: Stateful Instance Firewalls
screens.narratorSegment: Security Groups act as virtual, stateful firewalls attached to instances and other resources. Stateful means a Security Group tracks connection state: when you allow inbound traffic on a port, return traffic for that established connection is automatically permitted without an explicit outbound rule for that specific response. Practically, that lets you write concise rules: allow SSH inbound from your office IP and the return traffic is handled automatically. A concrete example: you add an ingress rule permitting TCP port 22 from 203.0.113.5/32. When that client connects, the Security Group allows the server's outbound return packets for that session even if you didn't add a separate egress rule for port 22. A common misconception is thinking Security Groups can deny traffic; they cannot. They only contain allow rules, and anything not explicitly allowed is implicitly denied. That means careful rule crafting is essential: accidentally allowing 0.0.0.0/0 for SSH is a security risk. Key takeaway: use Security Groups for fine-grained, instance-level access control and prefer referencing another Security Group for service-to-service access rather than broad CIDR ranges. Question to reflect on: when you allow inbound web traffic, what outbound rules must you add, if any, and why?

keyIdea.text: Security Groups track connections and only contain allow rules; use them for precise instance-level controls.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Security Groups: Stateful Instance Firewalls
Definition
Security Groups are attached to instances and resources, they are stateful and only allow traffic with explicit allow rules. Return traffic for an allowed connection is permitted automatically.
Key properties
  • Instance-level scope. Applies to network interfaces on instances and some managed resources.
  • Stateful: return traffic is automatically allowed.
  • Allow-only rules. Implicit deny otherwise.
Concrete example
Allow SSH from a single office IP. Use the Security Group ID as the source for database access from web servers instead of a CIDR.
Example Security Group rules
# Create a web server SG and allow HTTP and SSH (SSH limited to your IP)
aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name WebSG --description "Web Server Security Group" --vpc-id <YourVpcId>
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <WebSGId> --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <WebSGId> --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr <YourPublicIp>/32

# DB SG allowing MySQL from WebSG
aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name DBSG --description "Database SG" --vpc-id <YourVpcId>
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <DBSGId> --protocol tcp --port 3306 --source-group <WebSGId>
Key Takeaway

Security Groups keep rules concise by relying on state tracking; prefer SG references between tiers rather than open CIDRs.

Common Mistake
Allowing 0.0.0.0/0 for SSH exposes instances to brute force attacks.

screens.title: Configuring Security Group Rules
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring Security Group rules is a practical, repeatable process. First, define which ports and sources must reach an instance. Use the least-privilege principle: allow only the specific ports and the smallest CIDR or Security Group reference possible. A concrete walkthrough: create a WebSG that allows inbound HTTP on port 80 from anywhere and SSH on port 22 only from your office IP. Then create a DBSG that allows MySQL port 3306, but only when the source is the WebSG — not a broad CIDR. In the CLI example shown, I create Security Groups, add ingress rules, and reference the WebSG as a source for DBSG. A common misconception is that Security Groups require explicit egress for return traffic — they do not, because they are stateful; however explicit egress rules still matter when you intentionally restrict outbound traffic. Also be mindful that some managed services attach multiple network interfaces; place the SG on the interface used for the service traffic. Practical tip: tag Security Groups with names and purpose so teams know which SG to reference. Reflect: if a web server can reach the database only when using the WebSG ID as source, how would you audit which Security Groups are allowed to reach the DB?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Configuring Security Group Rules
Step-by-step pattern
  1. Identify required ports (example: 80, 443, 22, 3306).
  2. Decide trusted sources: single IP, CIDR, or another SG.
  3. Create SGs and add ingress rules. Leave egress open unless you must restrict outbound.
  4. Tag SGs with purpose and verify with a test connection.
Best practices
  • Prefer SG references for intra-VPC communication.
  • Limit SSH to known maintenance IPs or a bastion Security Group.
  • Document rule intent with tags and descriptions.
CLI code walkthrough
aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name WebSG --description "Web Server Security Group" --vpc-id <YourVpcId>
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <WebSGId> --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <WebSGId> --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr <YourPublicIp>/32

aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name DBSG --description "Database Security Group" --vpc-id <YourVpcId>
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <DBSGId> --protocol tcp --port 3306 --source-group <WebSGId>
Key Takeaway

Use least-privilege ingress rules and Security Group references for intra-VPC traffic to reduce attack surface.

Misconception
Stateful security means you never need egress rules — not true if you intentionally restrict outbound traffic for compliance.

screens.title: Common Security Group Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Even experienced engineers can make simple mistakes with Security Groups that lead to either security exposures or broken connectivity. One frequent error is opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0; this makes instances available to the public internet and exposes them to brute-force attacks. A better pattern is to restrict SSH to a specific IP range or to a bastion host Security Group. Another mistake is over-restricting egress without accounting for stateful return traffic to remote APIs or package repositories; limiting egress can unexpectedly break software updates or A P I calls. Developers sometimes assume Security Groups can deny traffic — they cannot — so they attempt to add deny rules and are surprised when the SG cannot express that intent. Use NACLs for explicit denies at the subnet level when you need to block known malicious ranges. Finally, a frequent operational gap is missing tags or descriptive rule descriptions; unclear security groups lead to improper re-use. The takeaway: build predictable, auditable SGs, avoid broad CIDRs, and document intent so the team can safely reference and reuse groups. Common Security Group Mistakes means don't open ssh to the world; use restricted sources and clear tags; don't expect deny rules in security groups.. In practical terms, pitfalls and how to avoid them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Common Security Group Mistakes
Mistake vs Fix
Opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 — Fix: restrict to your IP or a bastion SG.
Expecting deny rules in SG — Fix: use NACLs for explicit deny at subnet boundary.
Poor tagging and reuse — Fix: name SGs by role and include descriptive rule comments.
Pro Tip
When allowing service traffic, reference a Security Group as the source so that moving instances does not require IP updates.
Quick audit checklist
  • Search for SGs with 0.0.0.0/0 on sensitive ports.
  • Confirm SSH is limited to a maintenance IP or bastion SG.
  • Verify SG references between tiers for DB access.
Reflective Question

Which Security Group would you tighten first if you found a public CIDR on port 22, and why?

screens.title: Network ACLs (NACLs): Stateless Subnet Filters
screens.narratorSegment: Network ACLs are optional subnet-level firewalls that operate statelessly and process rules in numerical order. Stateless means that a NACL does not automatically allow return traffic for an allowed inbound flow; you must explicitly allow both directions. NACL entries are evaluated from the lowest rule number to the highest; as soon as a rule matches, that action is applied and rule processing stops. NACLs support both allow and deny actions, which makes them suitable for blocking known malicious IP ranges across an entire subnet. A concrete example: to allow HTTP into a public subnet you add an inbound allow for TCP port 80 and an outbound allow for ephemeral ports 1024–65535 so the return traffic from clients is permitted. A common misunderstanding is believing NACLs are redundant if Security Groups are configured — they are complementary. Use NACLs for coarse, fast-blocking at the subnet edge and Security Groups for fine-grained instance controls. Key takeaway: when a connection times out in a private subnet despite correct Security Group rules, check the NACL for missing outbound or ephemeral entries because stateless rules must cover both directions.

keyIdea.text: NACLs require explicit allow for both directions and process rules by number with the first match winning.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Network ACLs (NACLs): Stateless Subnet Filters
Definition
NACLs apply to subnets, are stateless, allow both explicit allow and deny entries, and evaluate rules in order.
Default NACL allows all traffic; custom NACLs typically start restrictive. Remember to add return rules for stateless traffic, or connections will time out.
Example behavior
Allow inbound TCP 80 (rule 100) and outbound ephemeral ports 1024–65535 (rule 110). If you forget the outbound ephemeral rule, client connections will hang despite inbound allowance.
NACL rule processing
  1. Rules are evaluated from lowest number to highest.
  2. On first match, the rule's action (allow or deny) is applied and processing stops.
  3. Implicit default: deny when no rule matches in a custom NACL.
Key Takeaway

When using NACLs, explicitly allow return traffic. Treat NACLs as broad filters and Security Groups as precise guards.

Pitfall
Forgetting to add both directions for a flow results in timeouts even when one direction is explicitly allowed.

screens.title: NACL Rule Ordering and Deny Rules
screens.narratorSegment: Designing effective NACLs is about order and explicit intent. Because NACLs evaluate rules by number from lowest to highest, place specific deny rules before broader allow rules. For example, if you need to block a known malicious IP range, add a deny rule with a lower number than your general allow rules. A concrete example: rule 50 denies 198.51.100.0/24, rule 100 allows HTTP and HTTPS, and rule 110 allows ephemeral ports for return traffic. Because the deny rule is evaluated first, traffic from that malicious range is blocked before any allow could match. Another important point: both ingress and egress sides of the NACL must be configured. For stateless return traffic, ensure ephemeral ports are allowed in the corresponding direction. A common misconception is thinking higher-numbered rules will override lower ones; they do not — the first match wins. Key takeaway: plan rule numbers methodically, document the purpose of denied ranges, and test with Flow Logs to confirm that the denied IPs are showing REJECT entries. How would you order rules if you needed to deny several small ranges but allow a broader corporate CIDR?

keyIdea.text: Place deny rules for bad IPs at lower numbers than general allow rules; configure both ingress and egress.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › NACL Rule Ordering and Deny Rules
Design pattern
Place specific deny rules at low numbers, then add allow rules for required protocols and port ranges, and finally include ephemeral port allowances for return traffic.
Document rule numbers and purpose so future maintainers do not insert rules that break intent.
Example rule set (conceptual)
Rule 50: Deny 198.51.100.0/24 (ingress). Rule 100: Allow TCP 80/443 (ingress). Rule 110: Allow TCP 1024-65535 (ingress) for return traffic.
Practical checklist
  • Identify IP ranges to block and assign low rule numbers.
  • Add specific allow rules for required services.
  • Add ephemeral port allowances for return traffic on both directions.
  • Test with VPC Flow Logs to ensure REJECTs appear for blocked ranges.
Reflective Question

If you add a deny for a malicious range after an allow rule, why might that fail to block traffic?

screens.title: Configuring NACLs for Public and Private Subnets
screens.narratorSegment: Applying NACLs to public and private subnets is a straightforward process when you follow consistent rule patterns. For a public subnet hosting web servers, you typically allow inbound HTTP and HTTPS and SSH where needed, and allow outbound symmetric ports for return traffic. In the example walkthrough you create a PublicNACL with inbound rules to allow 80, 443, and 22 and corresponding outbound rules plus ephemeral port allowances for return traffic. For private subnets, the pattern is narrower: allow MySQL from the web subnet CIDR and allow outbound HTTP/HTTPS to the NAT Gateway for software updates, plus ephemeral ports for return traffic. The CLI excerpts included in the lesson demonstrate creating NACLs and explicit create-network-acl-entry commands with rule numbers. Pitfall: do not forget the outbound ephemeral entries for return traffic. After creating rules, replace the subnet association to point to the new NACL and then test connectivity. The final verification step is to generate traffic and inspect Flow Logs to confirm ACCEPT or REJECT entries that match your rules. Configuring NACLs for Public and Private Subnets means public nacls allow web ports plus ephemeral ranges; private nacls allow service ports from trusted subnet cidrs and nat egress ports.. In practical terms, example rule sets and cli steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Configuring NACLs for Public and Private Subnets
Public subnet NACL pattern
Ingress: allow 80, 443, SSH (if needed). Egress: allow 80, 443, SSH, and ephemeral ports 1024–65535 for return traffic. Use rule numbers to keep denies before broad allows when blocking ranges.
Private subnet NACL pattern
Ingress: allow DB port from public subnet CIDR. Egress: allow HTTP/HTTPS to 0.0.0.0/0 via NAT and ephemeral return ports. Deny direct internet inbound access to private subnet.
CLI samples (conceptual)
# Create a NACL and add entries (concept)
aws ec2 create-network-acl --vpc-id <YourVpcId> --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=network-acl,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=PublicNACL}]'
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id <PublicNaclId> --rule-number 100 --protocol tcp --rule-action allow --ingress --port-range From=80,To=80 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id <PublicNaclId> --rule-number 110 --protocol tcp --rule-action allow --ingress --port-range From=1024,To=65535 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0

# Associate NACL with a subnet
aws ec2 replace-network-acl-association --association-id <PublicSubnetNaclAssociationId> --network-acl-id <PublicNaclId>
Key Takeaway

Match NACL rules to the subnet’s role and always include ephemeral port allowances for return traffic on both directions.

Common Mistake
Associating the wrong NACL with a subnet or forgetting the association replace step after creating custom NACLs.

screens.title: Combining Security Groups and NACLs
screens.narratorSegment: A layered approach uses NACLs as a coarse-grained boundary and Security Groups as fine-grained instance guards. Think of NACLs as the perimeter checkpoint that can quickly block a range, and Security Groups as the office-level guard providing strict port control. In practice, you might deploy a NACL on the public subnet that denies a malicious IP range and allows HTTP/HTTPS, while every web server has a Security Group that allows only ports 80 and 443 from anywhere and SSH only from a bastion SG or maintenance IP. For the private database subnet, the NACL denies internet inbound traffic and the DBSG allows MySQL only from the WebSG. This separation makes it easy to respond to threats: add a deny rule to the NACL to block a bad range at scale, and use Security Groups to rotate which hosts can access the DB. A misconception is to duplicate complex rules in both layers; instead, use NACLs for broad policies and SGs for per-resource policies. Test your design with Flow Logs to verify that undesirable traffic is REJECTED at the expected layer.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Combining Security Groups and NACLs
Pattern: public web + private DB
Public subnet NACL: allow 80/443, deny known bad ranges. WebSG: allow 80/443 from anywhere; SSH from bastion IP. Private subnet NACL: deny internet inbound; allow MySQL from web subnet CIDR. DBSG: allow MySQL only from WebSG.
Why this works
NACLs reduce attack surface at the subnet edge; Security Groups provide the detailed access controls that follow least privilege principles.
Decision checklist
  • Do you need to block an IP range across an entire subnet? Use a NACL deny.
  • Do you need to limit which servers can access a service? Use Security Group references.
  • Are you troubleshooting a connection failure? Check SG then NACL then Flow Logs.
Key Takeaway

Use each control for what it does best: NACLs for broad subnet filters and SGs for instance-level permissions.

screens.title: VPC Flow Logs: Capture and Interpret Traffic Metadata
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Flow Logs record metadata about IP traffic to and from network interfaces in your VPC, and are invaluable for diagnosing whether traffic was accepted or rejected. Flow Logs include the source and destination IPs, ports, protocol, bytes transferred, and the action field which reports ACCEPT or REJECT. They do not capture packet payloads, so they are a privacy-safe way to audit connectivity. A concrete troubleshooting scenario: an instance in a private subnet times out when contacting an external A P I. You confirm the instance Security Group allows outbound HTTPS. Flow Logs show REJECT entries for outbound port 443 originating from the instance. That indicates the NACL or another subnet-level control is denying the flow, not the instance SG. Another use is to confirm that a deny you added to a NACL is effectively blocking traffic at the subnet boundary by watching REJECTs from that source. Best practice: publish Flow Logs to CloudWatch Logs or S3 and filter on the VO attribute and the action. Closing question: when a Flow Log shows ACCEPT but your application still fails, which layers would you inspect next?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › VPC Flow Logs: Capture and Interpret Traffic Metadata
What Flow Logs contain
  • Source and destination IPs and ports
  • Protocol and byte counts
  • Action: ACCEPT or REJECT
Where to send logs
Send to CloudWatch Logs for real-time analysis or to S3 for long-term archival and batch analysis.
Troubleshooting flow
If a connection times out: check the instance SG first, then the subnet NACL, then the Flow Logs to see whether traffic was REJECTED at the subnet layer or never left the instance. Use the action field to decide which layer caused the block.

Flow Logs tell you whether traffic was accepted or rejected, which pinpoints the layer responsible for blocking connections.

screens.title: Hands-on: Secure a Web Server and Database
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through creating Security Groups and NACLs for a public web server and a private database server. Start by creating WebSG and DBSG following the CLI commands shown. For the public subnet, create a PublicNACL that allows 80/443 and SSH from your IP, and add ephemeral port rules for return traffic. For the private subnet, create a PrivateNACL that allows MySQL from the public subnet CIDR and allows HTTP/HTTPS outbound to the NAT Gateway, plus ephemeral ports for return traffic. After associating the NACLs with their subnets and launching EC2 instances into each subnet with the appropriate SG attached, run connectivity tests: SSH into the web server from your machine, attempt SSH directly to the database from your machine (should fail), SSH from web to DB (should work if DBSG allows WebSG), and from the DB try to reach the internet via ping or curl to confirm NAT egress. If any connectivity fails, consult Flow Logs and re-check that both directions are allowed on stateless NACLs. This exercise reinforces how the layers interact in real deployments.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Hands-on: Secure a Web Server and Database
Checklist
  1. Create WebSG and add ingress for 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 and 22 from your IP.
  2. Create DBSG allowing 3306 from WebSG.
  3. Create PublicNACL and PrivateNACL with appropriate allow/deny rules and ephemeral ports.
  4. Associate NACLs to subnets and launch instances with assigned SGs.
Test plan
  • SSH to web server from your IP — expect success.
  • SSH to DB from your IP — expect failure.
  • SSH from web to DB — expect success.
  • Ping or curl from DB to internet — expect success via NAT.
CLI snippets (starter)
# Create Security Groups and rules (use your VPC and IP values)
aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name WebSG --description "Web Server Security Group" --vpc-id <YourVpcId>
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <WebSGId> --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <WebSGId> --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr <YourPublicIp>/32

# Create NACL and add entries, then associate to subnet
aws ec2 create-network-acl --vpc-id <YourVpcId> --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=network-acl,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=PublicNACL}]'
# Add create-network-acl-entry commands for inbound/outbound rules as needed
Key Takeaway

Follow a create → associate → launch → test order and use Flow Logs to confirm whether flows are ACCEPTed or REJECTed.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Scenarios and Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: This assessment-style lesson helps you apply what you learned to real troubleshooting. Consider a private EC2 instance that cannot reach an external A P I on port 443. Security Group egress allows 443. The most likely cause is the subnet's NACL blocking outbound 443 or blocking the return ephemeral range. Inspect Flow Logs for the instance's ENI: if you see REJECT for flows with destination port 443, the NACL is blocking. Another scenario: a bastion host still cannot be reached even though its Security Group allows SSH from your IP. If Flow Logs show ACCEPT but the session fails, check instance-level OS firewall or route table misconfiguration. A second assessment question from the chapter asks which features to use to allow SSH from specific IPs but block known malicious ranges: use a Security Group to restrict SSH to the trusted IPs and a NACL to explicitly deny the malicious ranges at the subnet boundary. When you answer these questions, justify why the NACL is processed before instance-level considerations and how statefulness affects return traffic. Final reflective question: what log entry would convince you the NACL blocked a flow?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Troubleshooting Scenarios and Assessment
Scenario 1
Private instance times out to external API on 443 though SG allows egress. Inspect Flow Logs for REJECT entries. If REJECT appears, suspect NACL blocking outbound or missing ephemeral return rules.
Scenario 2
Bastion host unreachable despite SG allowing SSH and correct IP. If Flow Logs show ACCEPT, check OS firewall, route table, or instance service status — network controls may be fine but host-level services can fail.
Assessment Q
Which combination blocks a malicious IP range across a subnet but still allows SSH from specific IPs? Answer: NACL deny for the malicious range and Security Group allow for the specific SSH IP.
Key Takeaway

Use Flow Logs to confirm which layer produced a REJECT and then remediate at that layer rather than changing unrelated rules.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the core ideas. Security Groups are stateful, instance-level firewalls that contain allow rules only; return traffic for allowed connections is automatically permitted. Network ACLs are stateless, subnet-level filters that support allow and deny actions and evaluate rules by number, so the first matching rule applies. Use NACLs for broad, fast blocking such as denying known malicious ranges and Security Groups for precise, least-privilege access between tiers. VPC Flow Logs record metadata about traffic and include ACCEPT or REJECT flags that reveal which layer blocked a flow. When troubleshooting, check Security Groups first, then NACLs, and consult Flow Logs to confirm the blocking layer. Finally, always include ephemeral port allowances in NACLs for return traffic; forgetting those is a common cause of timeouts. These are practical, repeatable rules that will help you design and maintain secure VPC networks.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll build a mental model for how AWS protects network traffic inside your VPC. You'll learn the two complementary layers of defense: Security Groups, which guard individual instances and are stateful, and Network Access Control Lists, which guard entire subnets and are stateless. We'll also cover how VPC Flow Logs let you monitor ACCEPT and REJECT events, which is essential for diagnosing blocked traffic. Throughout, I’ll use a building security analogy: Security Groups are the guards on each office door, and NACLs are the checkpoints at a floor entrance. That analogy helps explain why one is stateful and the other is stateless, why Security Groups only have allow rules, and why NACLs support explicit denies and rule ordering. By the end of the chapter you will be able to design a simple secure architecture for a public web tier and a private database tier, configure the Security Groups and NACLs to match that design, and use Flow Logs to verify whether traffic is being accepted or rejected. Consider how a single rejected flow can show you whether the subnet boundary or the instance firewall is responsible — that distinction is the core insight we’ll practice.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish Security Groups from Network ACLs and choose the right tool for each use case. You will configure Security Groups to control inbound and outbound traffic for EC2 instances and other resources, and you will implement NACLs at the subnet boundary to add an extra stateless layer of defense. You will learn best practices for using both together so they reinforce rather than conflict, and you will enable and interpret VPC Flow Logs to verify whether traffic was accepted or rejected. Each objective builds practical capability: recognizing when a connection failure is due to a NACL rather than a Security Group, writing least-privilege rules for SSH and service ports, and designing a public web plus private database pattern that follows AWS best practice. These are hands-on skills you will practice with specific rule examples and a troubleshooting scenario, so you can both design secure networks and diagnose real connectivity problems quickly.

This second objectives screen emphasizes practice and troubleshooting. You will walk through a hands-on scenario that secures a web server in a public subnet and a database server in a private subnet, including Security Group and NACL configuration. You will validate connectivity: SSH to the web server from your IP, prevent direct SSH to the DB from the internet, allow web-to-db traffic from the web server’s Security Group, and validate private instances can reach the internet via a NAT Gateway. You will also learn a targeted troubleshooting question: when egress connections from a private instance time out despite Security Group egress allowing the port, learn to inspect NACLs and Flow Logs to find a stateless deny. Developing that troubleshooting habit — check SG then NACL then Flow Logs — will save time during incidents. Each objective is tied to a small verification step so you can confirm competency with a single test connection or a single flow log search.

Security Groups act as virtual, stateful firewalls attached to instances and other resources. Stateful means a Security Group tracks connection state: when you allow inbound traffic on a port, return traffic for that established connection is automatically permitted without an explicit outbound rule for that specific response. Practically, that lets you write concise rules: allow SSH inbound from your office IP and the return traffic is handled automatically. A concrete example: you add an ingress rule permitting TCP port 22 from 203.0.113.5/32. When that client connects, the Security Group allows the server's outbound return packets for that session even if you didn't add a separate egress rule for port 22. A common misconception is thinking Security Groups can deny traffic; they cannot. They only contain allow rules, and anything not explicitly allowed is implicitly denied. That means careful rule crafting is essential: accidentally allowing 0.0.0.0/0 for SSH is a security risk. Key takeaway: use Security Groups for fine-grained, instance-level access control and prefer referencing another Security Group for service-to-service access rather than broad CIDR ranges. Question to reflect on: when you allow inbound web traffic, what outbound rules must you add, if any, and why?

Configuring Security Group rules is a practical, repeatable process. First, define which ports and sources must reach an instance. Use the least-privilege principle: allow only the specific ports and the smallest CIDR or Security Group reference possible. A concrete walkthrough: create a WebSG that allows inbound HTTP on port 80 from anywhere and SSH on port 22 only from your office IP. Then create a DBSG that allows MySQL port 3306, but only when the source is the WebSG — not a broad CIDR. In the CLI example shown, I create Security Groups, add ingress rules, and reference the WebSG as a source for DBSG. A common misconception is that Security Groups require explicit egress for return traffic — they do not, because they are stateful; however explicit egress rules still matter when you intentionally restrict outbound traffic. Also be mindful that some managed services attach multiple network interfaces; place the SG on the interface used for the service traffic. Practical tip: tag Security Groups with names and purpose so teams know which SG to reference. Reflect: if a web server can reach the database only when using the WebSG ID as source, how would you audit which Security Groups are allowed to reach the DB?

Even experienced engineers can make simple mistakes with Security Groups that lead to either security exposures or broken connectivity. One frequent error is opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0; this makes instances available to the public internet and exposes them to brute-force attacks. A better pattern is to restrict SSH to a specific IP range or to a bastion host Security Group. Another mistake is over-restricting egress without accounting for stateful return traffic to remote APIs or package repositories; limiting egress can unexpectedly break software updates or A P I calls. Developers sometimes assume Security Groups can deny traffic — they cannot — so they attempt to add deny rules and are surprised when the SG cannot express that intent. Use NACLs for explicit denies at the subnet level when you need to block known malicious ranges. Finally, a frequent operational gap is missing tags or descriptive rule descriptions; unclear security groups lead to improper re-use. The takeaway: build predictable, auditable SGs, avoid broad CIDRs, and document intent so the team can safely reference and reuse groups. Common Security Group Mistakes means don't open ssh to the world; use restricted sources and clear tags; don't expect deny rules in security groups.. In practical terms, pitfalls and how to avoid them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Network ACLs are optional subnet-level firewalls that operate statelessly and process rules in numerical order. Stateless means that a NACL does not automatically allow return traffic for an allowed inbound flow; you must explicitly allow both directions. NACL entries are evaluated from the lowest rule number to the highest; as soon as a rule matches, that action is applied and rule processing stops. NACLs support both allow and deny actions, which makes them suitable for blocking known malicious IP ranges across an entire subnet. A concrete example: to allow HTTP into a public subnet you add an inbound allow for TCP port 80 and an outbound allow for ephemeral ports 1024–65535 so the return traffic from clients is permitted. A common misunderstanding is believing NACLs are redundant if Security Groups are configured — they are complementary. Use NACLs for coarse, fast-blocking at the subnet edge and Security Groups for fine-grained instance controls. Key takeaway: when a connection times out in a private subnet despite correct Security Group rules, check the NACL for missing outbound or ephemeral entries because stateless rules must cover both directions.

Designing effective NACLs is about order and explicit intent. Because NACLs evaluate rules by number from lowest to highest, place specific deny rules before broader allow rules. For example, if you need to block a known malicious IP range, add a deny rule with a lower number than your general allow rules. A concrete example: rule 50 denies 198.51.100.0/24, rule 100 allows HTTP and HTTPS, and rule 110 allows ephemeral ports for return traffic. Because the deny rule is evaluated first, traffic from that malicious range is blocked before any allow could match. Another important point: both ingress and egress sides of the NACL must be configured. For stateless return traffic, ensure ephemeral ports are allowed in the corresponding direction. A common misconception is thinking higher-numbered rules will override lower ones; they do not — the first match wins. Key takeaway: plan rule numbers methodically, document the purpose of denied ranges, and test with Flow Logs to confirm that the denied IPs are showing REJECT entries. How would you order rules if you needed to deny several small ranges but allow a broader corporate CIDR?

Applying NACLs to public and private subnets is a straightforward process when you follow consistent rule patterns. For a public subnet hosting web servers, you typically allow inbound HTTP and HTTPS and SSH where needed, and allow outbound symmetric ports for return traffic. In the example walkthrough you create a PublicNACL with inbound rules to allow 80, 443, and 22 and corresponding outbound rules plus ephemeral port allowances for return traffic. For private subnets, the pattern is narrower: allow MySQL from the web subnet CIDR and allow outbound HTTP/HTTPS to the NAT Gateway for software updates, plus ephemeral ports for return traffic. The CLI excerpts included in the lesson demonstrate creating NACLs and explicit create-network-acl-entry commands with rule numbers. Pitfall: do not forget the outbound ephemeral entries for return traffic. After creating rules, replace the subnet association to point to the new NACL and then test connectivity. The final verification step is to generate traffic and inspect Flow Logs to confirm ACCEPT or REJECT entries that match your rules. Configuring NACLs for Public and Private Subnets means public nacls allow web ports plus ephemeral ranges; private nacls allow service ports from trusted subnet cidrs and nat egress ports.. In practical terms, example rule sets and cli steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Best practice: publish Flow Logs to CloudWatch Logs or S3 and filter on the VO attribute and the action. Closing question: when a Flow Log shows ACCEPT but your application still fails, which layers would you inspect next?

This hands-on activity walks you through creating Security Groups and NACLs for a public web server and a private database server. Start by creating WebSG and DBSG following the CLI commands shown. For the public subnet, create a PublicNACL that allows 80/443 and SSH from your IP, and add ephemeral port rules for return traffic. For the private subnet, create a PrivateNACL that allows MySQL from the public subnet CIDR and allows HTTP/HTTPS outbound to the NAT Gateway, plus ephemeral ports for return traffic. After associating the NACLs with their subnets and launching EC2 instances into each subnet with the appropriate SG attached, run connectivity tests: SSH into the web server from your machine, attempt SSH directly to the database from your machine (should fail), SSH from web to DB (should work if DBSG allows WebSG), and from the DB try to reach the internet via ping or curl to confirm NAT egress. If any connectivity fails, consult Flow Logs and re-check that both directions are allowed on stateless NACLs. This exercise reinforces how the layers interact in real deployments.

This assessment-style lesson helps you apply what you learned to real troubleshooting. Consider a private EC2 instance that cannot reach an external A P I on port 443. Security Group egress allows 443. The most likely cause is the subnet's NACL blocking outbound 443 or blocking the return ephemeral range. Inspect Flow Logs for the instance's ENI: if you see REJECT for flows with destination port 443, the NACL is blocking. Another scenario: a bastion host still cannot be reached even though its Security Group allows SSH from your IP. If Flow Logs show ACCEPT but the session fails, check instance-level OS firewall or route table misconfiguration. A second assessment question from the chapter asks which features to use to allow SSH from specific IPs but block known malicious ranges: use a Security Group to restrict SSH to the trusted IPs and a NACL to explicitly deny the malicious ranges at the subnet boundary. When you answer these questions, justify why the NACL is processed before instance-level considerations and how statefulness affects return traffic. Final reflective question: what log entry would convince you the NACL blocked a flow?

Let's summarize the core ideas. Security Groups are stateful, instance-level firewalls that contain allow rules only; return traffic for allowed connections is automatically permitted. Network ACLs are stateless, subnet-level filters that support allow and deny actions and evaluate rules by number, so the first matching rule applies. Use NACLs for broad, fast blocking such as denying known malicious ranges and Security Groups for precise, least-privilege access between tiers. VPC Flow Logs record metadata about traffic and include ACCEPT or REJECT flags that reveal which layer blocked a flow. When troubleshooting, check Security Groups first, then NACLs, and consult Flow Logs to confirm the blocking layer. Finally, always include ephemeral port allowances in NACLs for return traffic; forgetting those is a common cause of timeouts. These are practical, repeatable rules that will help you design and maintain secure VPC networks.

Three concise reminders to carry forward: first, Security Groups are stateful and only express allow rules; use them for instance-level least privilege. Second, NACLs are stateless, support allow and deny, and evaluate rules numerically — put denies early. Third, VPC Flow Logs record ACCEPT and REJECT metadata; use them to identify whether the subnet boundary or instance firewall blocked a connection. These three ideas form a fast mental checklist: decide where to put rules, be explicit about return traffic for stateless controls, and verify with logs before changing rules unnecessarily. That checklist reduces troubleshooting time and reduces accidental exposure when configuring production networks.
